s1-l032-neutrino-mass-pmns-majorana.rubric: Full credit requires: the PMNS matrix relates flavour eigenstates to mass eigenstates (a unitary mixing matrix with three angles and a phase); oscillations depend on mass-squared differences and so require masses; evidence includes atmospheric (muon neutrino disappearance) and solar neutrino experiments.
s1-l032-neutrino-mass-pmns-majorana.modelAnswer:
The PMNS matrix is the unitary matrix that expresses each flavour state ($
u_e,
u_\mu,
u_	au$) as a superposition of mass eigenstates, with three mixing angles and a CP phase. Because oscillation probabilities depend on differences of mass squared, observing atmospheric muon-neutrino disappearance and solar neutrino conversion shows that at least two neutrinos have different, hence non-zero, masses.

s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.prompt: Requiring the Dirac Lagrangian to be invariant under a position-dependent phase change $\psi\to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi$ forces what addition?
options: A scalar field that gives the electron a mass
A vector field $A_\mu$ (the photon) coupled through $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+iqA_\mu$
A change of the electron charge to a complex number
Nothing; the Dirac Lagrangian is already invariant under local phase changes
s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.explanation: The derivative term acquires an extra piece $\partial_\mu\alpha$, breaking invariance. Introducing $A_\mu\to A_\mu-\partial_\mu\alpha/q$ in the covariant derivative cancels it. Demanding local gauge invariance thus produces electromagnetism.

s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.prompt: Why do gluons interact directly with each other while photons do not?
options: Gluons are much heavier than photons and so interact more
Gluons carry colour charge, whereas the photon is electrically neutral
Photons obey the Pauli principle, so they cannot interact with each other
Gluons are always virtual, so they can be exchanged between themselves
s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.explanation: In a non-Abelian gauge theory the gauge bosons transform under the group and carry its charge, giving three- and four-gluon vertices (and the self-interaction of $W^\pm$ and $Z$). The photon has no electric charge, so photons do not directly scatter off each other at tree level.

s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.prompt: Explain the gauge principle: how demanding invariance under a position-dependent phase change forces a massless photon field into the Dirac Lagrangian.
s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.rubric: Full credit requires: $\partial_\mu\psi$ picks up an extra term $i\partial_\mu\alpha\,\psi$ under a local phase change; to cancel it, replace $\partial_\mu$ by $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+iqA_\mu$ with $A_\mu\to A_\mu-\partial_\mu\alpha/q$; this introduces a vector field coupled to the current, the photon; a mass term $A_\mu A^\mu$ is not invariant, so it is massless.
s1-l033-local-gauge-invariance-yang-mill.modelAnswer: Under $\psi\to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi$ the derivative produces an unwanted term $i(\partial_\mu\alpha)\psi$. To restore invariance one introduces a vector field with $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+iqA_\mu$ and $A_\mu\to A_\mu-\partial_\mu\alpha/q$, so the extra terms cancel. The new field is the photon, whose coupling to the charge current is fixed, and a mass term $A_\mu A^\mu$ would break the invariance, so it is massless.

s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.prompt: In electroweak theory $m_W=m_Z\cos\theta_W$. With $m_Z=91.19$ GeV and $\sin^2\theta_W=0.2229$ (on-shell definition), find $m_W$ in GeV.
s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.explanation: $\cos\theta_W=\sqrt{1-0.2229}=0.8816$, so $m_W=91.19\times0.8816\approx80.4$ GeV, close to the measured 80.38 GeV.

s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.prompt: Why can't we simply add a mass term $\tfrac12m_W^2W_\mu W^\mu$ for the $W$ boson by hand?
options: It breaks the SU(2) gauge invariance of the theory
It would make the $W$ boson electrically charged and unstable
A mass term of this kind violates electric charge conservation
It would make the $W$ travel at the speed of light
s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.explanation: Under local gauge transformations $W_\mu$ shifts by a derivative term, so $W_\mu W^\mu$ is not invariant. A theory with explicit massive vector bosons is non-renormalisable and violates unitarity at high energy. The Higgs mechanism provides masses while preserving gauge invariance in the Lagrangian.

s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.prompt: Explain in your own words how the photon and $Z$ boson arise as mixtures of the SU(2) and U(1) gauge fields, and what the weak mixing angle measures.
s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.rubric: Full credit requires: the electroweak theory has $W^1,W^2,W^3$ (SU(2) with coupling g) and $B$ (U(1) with g'); the neutral fields $W^3$ and $B$ mix into the massless photon $A=B\cos\theta_W+W^3\sin\theta_W$ and the massive $Z=-B\sin\theta_W+W^3\cos\theta_W$; $\tan\theta_W=g'/g$ and $e=g\sin\theta_W$, so the electromagnetic coupling is a combination of the two; the angle measures the mixing (and relates $m_W=m_Z\cos\theta_W$).
s1-l034-electroweak-su2-u1-mass-problem.modelAnswer: The theory has an SU(2) triplet $W^{1,2,3}$ with coupling $g$ and a U(1) field $B$ with coupling $g'$. After symmetry breaking, the neutral fields $W^3$ and $B$ rotate into the mass eigenstates: the massless photon $A=B\cos\theta_W+W^3\sin\theta_W$ and the massive $Z=W^3\cos\theta_W-B\sin\theta_W$. The weak mixing angle satisfies $\tan\theta_W=g'/g$, gives $e=g\sin\theta_W$, and relates the boson masses by $m_W=m_Z\cos\theta_W$. Electromagnetism and the weak force are thus two faces of one interaction.

s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.prompt: In the Higgs mechanism, what happens to the Goldstone bosons that appear when the electroweak symmetry is spontaneously broken?
options: They remain as massless particles that have been observed at the LHC
They become the Higgs boson itself once symmetry breaks
They decay into photon pairs before they can be detected
They become the longitudinal polarisations of the $W^\pm$ and $Z$
s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.explanation: A massless gauge boson has two polarisations; a massive one has three. The extra (longitudinal) degree of freedom comes from the Goldstone mode. Three Goldstone modes become the longitudinal $W^+,W^-,Z$, and one scalar remains: the Higgs boson.

s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.prompt: The top-quark Yukawa coupling is $y_t=\sqrt2\,m_t/v$, from $m_f=y_fv/\sqrt2$. With $m_t=172.7$ GeV and $v=246.2$ GeV, find $y_t$.
s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.explanation: $y_t=1.414\times172.7/246.2\approx0.99$: remarkably close to 1. The electron's coupling is $\approx3\times10^{-6}$; why the Yukawa couplings span such a range is the 'flavour puzzle'.

s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.prompt: Explain how the Higgs mechanism gives mass to the $W$ and $Z$ bosons and to fermions without violating gauge invariance of the Lagrangian.
s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.rubric: Full credit requires: the Lagrangian (with a Higgs doublet and a Mexican-hat potential) is gauge invariant but the lowest-energy state has a non-zero vacuum expectation value $v$ (spontaneous symmetry breaking); expanding about the vacuum, the gauge-boson kinetic terms $|D_\mu\phi|^2$ produce mass terms $\propto g^2v^2$; fermion Yukawa couplings $y\bar\psi\phi\psi$ become masses $yv/\sqrt2$; no explicit mass term is ever put in the Lagrangian.
s1-l035-ssb-higgs-mechanism.modelAnswer: The Lagrangian contains no explicit mass terms and is gauge invariant. It includes a Higgs doublet with a Mexican-hat potential, whose minimum is at a non-zero field value $v\approx246$ GeV, so the vacuum itself breaks the symmetry. Expanding around the vacuum, the gauge-field coupling $|D_\mu\phi|^2$ contains terms $\propto g^2v^2W_\mu W^\mu$, which are $W$ and $Z$ masses, and the Yukawa couplings $y_f\bar\psi\psi\phi$ become fermion masses $y_fv/\sqrt2$. The symmetry is hidden (spontaneously broken) in the vacuum, not violated in the equations.

s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.prompt: Which decay mode of a 125 GeV Higgs boson is most probable?
options: $H\to\gamma\gamma$ (about 50%)
$H\to e^+e^-$, since electrons are the lightest charged particles
$H\to b\bar b$ (about 58%)
$H\to t\bar t$, since the top is the heaviest quark
s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.explanation: The top quark is heavier than $m_H/2$, so $t\bar t$ is kinematically forbidden. The $H\to\gamma\gamma$ (0.2%) and $ZZ\to4\ell$ (0.01%) channels are rare but clean, so they were the discovery modes in 2012. $H\to e^+e^-$ is minuscule because the coupling scales with the electron mass.

s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.prompt: Which of the following observations cannot be accommodated by the original (minimal) Standard Model?
options: The existence of the Higgs boson
The masses of the $W$ and $Z$ bosons
Neutrino oscillations
The decay rate of the muon
s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.explanation: The minimal SM has massless neutrinos. Other open problems: the nature of dark matter (about 27% of the universe), the matter-antimatter asymmetry, the hierarchy problem (why the Higgs mass is so far below the Planck scale), and gravity.

s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.prompt: The decay $H\to\gamma\gamma$ has a branching ratio of only about 0.2%. Why was it a discovery channel at the LHC?
options: Photon pairs give a clean, narrow mass peak over a smooth background
It is the most probable Higgs decay and so dominates
The Higgs couples most strongly to photons of all particles
Photons are the only particles the detectors can measure
s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.explanation: The dominant decay $H\to b\bar b$ is swamped by QCD background, whereas two energetic photons can be measured precisely, so the $m_{\gamma\gamma}$ distribution shows a narrow bump near 125 GeV on a smooth falling background.

s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.prompt: Name two phenomena that the minimal Standard Model cannot explain, and say briefly what is missing in each case.
s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.rubric: Full credit requires: two valid open problems such as neutrino masses (SM neutrinos massless), dark matter (no candidate particle), matter-antimatter asymmetry (insufficient CP violation), or the hierarchy problem (why the Higgs mass is so far below the Planck scale), each with one sentence on what is missing.
s1-l036-higgs-phenomenology-open-problem.modelAnswer: Neutrino masses: the minimal Standard Model has no right-handed neutrinos or mass term, yet oscillations require non-zero masses. Dark matter: about 85% of the matter in the universe is non-luminous, and no Standard Model particle has the right properties. (Others: baryon asymmetry, which needs far more CP violation, and the hierarchy problem of the Higgs mass.)
